summary: Teach nets as the visible 2-D↔3-D relationship by having children PREDICT whether a flat arrangement of squares will fold into a cube, then fold to check. Build structural reasoning by anchoring on a base face, tracking composites (a 'line of four squares' wraps the cube's sides while the remaining two cap top and bottom, in nets that contain such a line), and mapping net features to solid features (each shape→a face; each fold line→an edge, while pairs of outer sides join to make the remaining edges; several corner points of the net meet at each vertex). The central goal is to move children from judging by whether a net 'looks like the usual one' to reasoning from structure — accepting unfamiliar valid nets (a cube has eleven), rejecting arrangements whose layout cannot close, and producing a genuinely new valid net.
misconceptions: Only the familiar T/cross net makes a cube (prototype-as-only-net; Mariotti 1989) — other valid nets are rejected and near-prototypes trusted.
Any arrangement with the right number of faces folds up — attends to face count, not arrangement.
Cannot predict the fold direction of an L-shape, so mis-assigns which faces meet — a face is thought 'stuck in the corner' or two squares that should be opposite are left adjacent.

activities.title: Predict then fold: does this arrangement close into a cube?
steps: Look at a flat arrangement of six squares and, before folding, commit to a prediction: 'will this fold into a closed cube?' and say WHY.

Fold the arrangement (physical card/Polydron cut-outs, or by folding a paper net) to check the prediction — treating the card as a stand-in for the ideal flat net and asking about the cube it would form, not about the card as an object.
Start with the familiar cross/T net, then meet an unfamiliar 'staircase' zig-zag (2-2-2) net and predict it before folding.
Fold the staircase and observe that it ALSO closes into a cube, with every face covered once and no face left open (allowing for slight gaps from card thickness).
Try a 2-by-3 block of six squares: predict, fold, and watch squares overlap onto the same face while other cube faces are left uncovered.
activities.insight: Whether a net closes into a cube is decided by the ARRANGEMENT of the squares, not merely by having six of them. Unfamiliar nets can be valid and prototype-looking blocks can fail.

activities.title: Anchor a base and track where every square lands
steps: Choose one square as the base face and fold the others up around it.

Where the net contains one (as in the cross/1-4-1 layout), identify the 'line of four squares' that wraps to form the sides, then place the remaining two as top and bottom; for other valid layouts such as the 2-2-2 staircase, track each individual square's destination from the base instead.
For an L-shape or line arrangement, predict the fold direction and name which two squares end up on OPPOSITE faces before folding.
After folding, point to the two squares that face each other across the cube and explain how you know they never touch.
activities.insight: Anchoring on a base face and tracking where each square lands (using composites like a line of four when the net has one) lets you predict which faces meet and which become opposite, reducing the amount you have to hold in your head at once.

activities.title: Make it fail, then make a new one
steps: Starting from a valid net, slide ONE square to a new spot and predict whether it still folds into a cube; fold to check and describe what goes wrong when it fails.
Turn a valid net into a DIFFERENT valid net by moving just one square.
Draw a genuinely different arrangement of six squares that also folds into a cube (e.g. a 1-4-1 or 2-2-2 layout) and map each square to the cube face it becomes.

Map net features to solid features: each square→a face; each shared side (fold line)→an edge, and each pair of outer sides that join when folded→one more edge; several corner points of the net come together at each vertex (count them: 12 edges and 8 vertices on the cube).
activities.insight: Producing a new valid net and explaining why a moved square breaks or preserves the fold shows structural understanding that cannot be faked by matching the prototype.

activities.title: Extend the reasoning to other solids
steps: Draw and fold (mentally or physically) the net of a cuboid and a triangular prism, checking which faces connect.
Build a 3-D shape from its net and verify that all faces, edges, and vertices match.
Sketch a net of a square-based pyramid from a description or a 3-D model, transferring the base-and-fold reasoning from the cube.
Given several nets for one target solid, identify which fold correctly and explain why the others won't.
activities.insight: The same strategy — anchor a base, track how faces wrap, check faces/edges/vertices — applies beyond the cube to cuboids, prisms and pyramids.

checkQuestion: Here are three flat arrangements of six squares: the usual cross-shaped net, a 2-by-3 block of six squares, and a 'staircase' zig-zag net. For each one, tell me whether it will fold into a closed cube and how you know — point to which square becomes the top and which two faces end up opposite each other. Then draw me a different arrangement of six squares that also folds into a cube.
checkAnswer: Accepts the cross and the staircase as valid and rejects the 2-by-3 block; justifies by imagined folding anchored to a base face — tracking which squares wrap to the sides and which two become top and bottom / opposite faces, not by resemblance to a 'usual' net — and draws a fourth genuinely different valid net (e.g. a 1-4-1 or 2-2-2 arrangement) mapping its squares to cube faces.
